title: Slink and the Sparkly Secret
markdown:
In the silver passes of Cloudneedle Ridge the pines kept their own weather, and a young wizard named Peregrin kept a lizard who would not keep his hands — or rather his hats — to himself. Peregrin’s robes always seemed a little too long, trailing like moonlight wisps, and a sprinkle of stardust lived in his hair as if it had nowhere better to be. Slink was quick and mischievous, beady eyes full of spark, and he loved to snatch hats. The floppy wizard hat with the little moon on the brim? Zip. Gone. The cozy wool cap? Zip. Even a fun feathered beret. Slink would flick his long tail and a hat would disappear, usually to the highest tippy-top branch of the tallest pine, waving like a silly flag.

“Slink,” Peregrin would sigh, voice like a dry leaf skittering. “Where are you taking them? They just wobble.”

Slink would blink, tilt his head, and flick his tongue as if to say it was a mystery. A very important lizard mystery.

One blustery afternoon a whisper tickled the ridge. The squirrels chattered with excitement. The rumour was shimmering hat-stealing sprites in the woods. “Sprites,” Peregrin murmured. He looked at Slink, who was already eyeing his spare pointy hat, tail twitching. “Or perhaps something else.” Curiosity lit like a match that had been waiting in a pocket.

Peregrin loved mysteries, and this one involved his own hat-stealing lizard. He tied his long robe. “Come on, Slink. Let’s go find those sprites. And maybe get a hat or two back.” Slink was already trying to climb into his pocket.

The Whispering Woods lived up to its name. Wind sang a soft whispery song through pine needles. Sunlight dappled the mossy ground into a golden quilt. Peregrin saw strange things: little piles of shiny pebbles in neat circles; the sweet smell of warm honey though no flowers were blooming. Then a glint, a flash of something shiny darting behind feathery ferns, fast as a sunbeam that had decided to be a rainbow.

“Did you see that?” he whispered, heart beating like a hummingbird’s wings. Slink, surprisingly, did not try to snatch the hat. He sat on Peregrin’s shoulder, little claws gripping the robe, and watched the ferns too. Even Slink seemed amazed.

A tiny tinkling, like little bells, came from behind the ferns. Then a creature tumbled out, no bigger than Peregrin’s hand. Scales shimmered like wet river stones. Delicate see-through wings that held their own quiet light. It looked like a dragon, but a tiny, tiny one.

Peregrin’s eyes went wide. A tickle of delight, like the first sip of fizzy lemonade.

The tiny dragon looked startled. Big liquid eyes blinked. It had a bright red shiny button in its mouth and tried to wear it on its snout, but it kept slipping. Tinkle-tinkle, it whimpered. The button fell to the soft ground.

Peregrin knelt slowly. “Hello,” he said, soft as a falling feather. “Are you all right? That button looks tricky.”

The tiny dragon tilted its head. Wings fluttered. “R-rumble-purr,” it chirped, a soft rumbling sound. It nudged the button with its nose. A sad little puff of smoke came out.

Then Peregrin understood. The sprites were not sprites. They were this little dragon. He would soon learn its name was Pepplewing. Pepplewing loved shiny things more than anything. And Slink? Slink was not stealing hats to be naughty. He was collecting them. Pepplewing was too small to reach the shiny bits on the hats. Slink, in his own way, was helping the little dragon find treasures.

Pepplewing nudged the button again. Slink hopped down from Peregrin’s shoulder and nudged it toward Pepplewing. Then he looked at Peregrin. With a surprising flick of his tail, Slink nudged the spare pointy hat. The silver buckle glinted in the sun.

Pepplewing’s eyes lit. A tiny puff of smoke swirled. He reached for the buckle with tiny claws. Slink nudged the hat again. A happy rumbling purr, like a tiny kitten. He hooked a claw around the buckle. The shiny metal gleamed on his scales.

Peregrin smiled. “It wasn’t sprites. It was a little dragon who loved shiny things. And you were helping him find them.” He helped Pepplewing carefully place the shiny button on a vine. It made a perfect tiny helmet that sat jauntily on his head. Pepplewing chirped. Slink trotted over and nudged Peregrin’s shoe, asking for a scratch.

As the sun dipped behind the mountains and painted the sky purple and orange, they walked back. Peregrin wore his hat. Slink trotted beside him, tail flicking proudly. Pepplewing, sparkly button-helmet and all, fluttered nearby, and sometimes landed on Slink’s back for a quick exciting ride.

The rumour of hat-snatching sprites faded like mist. What remained was a young wizard, a helpful lizard, and a tiny dragon who loved sparkle, walking the same path as if they had always meant to share it. Slink did not snatch the moon-brim hat that evening. He had already found the secret it was for.
